result:
The rain started on a Tuesday, the way important things always do—without announcement, without permission. I was seven, maybe eight, sitting cross-legged on the kitchen floor with a box of crayons and a coloring book that had already been colored in twice. My mother stood at the window watching the sky bruise into something darker, and I remember she didn't say anything. She just stood there with her coffee getting cold in her hands, and I thought, even then, that the cold coffee was important. That it meant something.

I still don't know what.

There's a particular shade of green that only exists in late October, when the light is slanted and the leaves haven't quite given up but they know they're going to. I used to chase that color as a kid, trying to capture it in drawings that never worked. Crayola had ninety of them back then, and none of them were right. I wonder if anyone has ever successfully painted October. I suspect not. Some things resist being held.

My grandmother kept a garden that never quite took off. The soil was wrong, she said, or the light, or her own brown thumb. But she kept at it, year after year, planting tomatoes that grew stunted and peppers that came in bitter. I asked her once why she bothered, and she looked at me like I'd asked why people breathe. "Because the trying is the thing," she said. "The trying is the whole point." I was maybe twelve, and I didn't understand. Now I'm thirty-four, and I think I'm starting to.

There's a coffee shop on the corner of Elm and something-or-other that I've been going to for six years. The barista knows my order, which feels like a small failure of identity. I used to be someone who experimented. Now I'm someone who orders the same oat milk cortado every morning at 7:15, and I read the same three pages of a book I'll never finish, and the light comes through the window in a way I've memorized. I tell myself this is comfort. Some days I almost believe it.

My father called me last week, which he does now—calls me, I mean, as a verb, a separate action. For years he just was, the way a wall is or a floor, something you move around without thinking. Then he became a person who calls, which is somehow worse. We talked about nothing. The weather. A neighbor's dog. The price of eggs, which has become the universal small talk of our particular moment. When we hung up I stood in my kitchen for a long time, holding my phone like it was a small animal I didn't know what to do with.

I keep a list in my head of things I want to remember, but the list keeps changing. I used to want to remember the names of all the kids in my third-grade class. Now I can only remember Maya, who had braids, and David, who cried once during a fire drill for reasons no one ever explained. I used to want to remember the words to every song I loved. Now they're all gone except the hooks, the parts that weren't really the songs at all but the scaffolding around them. Memory is a leaky vessel. We pour and pour and the level never rises.

There's a woman who walks her dog past my apartment every evening around six. Golden retriever, old and slow, walks with a slight limp. She always smiles at me through the window, and I always smile back, and we have been doing this for two years without exchanging a single word. I find this comforting in a way I can't fully explain. It's proof, maybe, that we can share something without it needing to become anything else. That recognition can be its own currency.

I spent most of my twenties trying to become someone. Some version of a person I thought I was supposed to be—more accomplished, more certain, more anything. I read the books I was supposed to read and listened to the music I was supposed to like and had the opinions I was supposed to have. Then somewhere in my early thirties I got tired, and the tiredness turned into something else, and now I'm just here. Just a person in a body in a room in a building in a city in a country on a planet. The bigness of it used to frighten me. Now it mostly just feels true.

I think about death sometimes, but not in the way people mean when they say they think about death. I mean the smaller deaths. The way the version of you that existed last year is already gone, unreachable, and the one from five years ago is even more so. We are all of us dying continuously into who we were. I find this either comforting or terrifying depending on the day. Usually both.

My favorite sound is rain on a window when I'm warm inside and don't have to go anywhere. My favorite smell is the inside of a book, old and dusty and slightly sweet. My favorite feeling is the moment just before sleep, when the thoughts start to unspool and the boundary between me and not-me gets soft. I've been trying to live more inside these small preferences, these tiny yeses. The world is loud and demands so much. I'd rather be quiet and notice things.

I don't know what this is, exactly. A letter to no one. A list of things I've noticed. A proof of something—I don't know what. That I'm here, maybe. That I was paying attention, some of the time, anyway. That the cold coffee mattered, and the green that couldn't be captured, and the woman with the golden retriever, and my father's voice on the phone saying nothing in particular.

The rain probably stopped by now. I haven't looked.
